notes.meaning: About four months had passed since Nehemiah heard the bad news about Jerusalem. As the king's trusted cupbearer, he served wine at the royal table. Persian court rules required servants to look happy, so Nehemiah had never shown sorrow before the king until now.

King Artaxerxes noticed Nehemiah's gloom and asked what was troubling his heart, since he was not physically sick. This kindly question terrified Nehemiah. Showing sadness in front of the monarch was forbidden and could easily be mistaken for discontent or disloyalty.

Nehemiah began with a polite wish for the king's long life and then spoke honestly about his grief. He wisely described Jerusalem as the city where his ancestors were buried rather than naming the city outright. The Persians had deep respect for graves, so this touched the king's heart.

The king asked Nehemiah what he wanted him to do. Before saying a word, Nehemiah shot up a silent, quick prayer to God for help and favor. His four months of earlier prayer prepared him to make this instant appeal in a moment of great need.

Nehemiah humbly presented his request, asking the king to send him to Judah to rebuild the city of his fathers' tombs. He asked not merely for permission to visit, but for royal backing to carry out the work. He focused on restoring his ancestral home rather than making a political speech.

The king sat with his queen beside him and asked how long the journey would take and when Nehemiah would return. Because Nehemiah had already planned carefully during his months of waiting, he gave the king a set time. Pleased with the plan, the king granted him leave to go.

Nehemiah then asked for official royal letters to the governors of the provinces west of the Euphrates River. These letters would guarantee him safe passage through foreign territories on the way to Judah. He wisely sought proper protection before embarking on the dangerous journey.

Nehemiah also asked for an order to the keeper of the king's forest for timber to repair the gates, the city walls, and his own residence. The king granted every request. Nehemiah gave all the credit to God, recognizing that the Lord's kind and powerful hand had guided the king's heart.

Nehemiah traveled west, reached the regional governors, and delivered the royal letters. The king also sent Persian army officers and cavalry along with him for protection and honor. This royal guard showed everyone that Nehemiah had the full support of the emperor.

Local leaders named Sanballat and Tobiah were deeply upset when they learned about Nehemiah's arrival. They hated the idea that anyone had come to help the people of Israel and improve their condition. Opposition often begins as soon as God's servants start taking real action.

Nehemiah safely reached Jerusalem and rested there for three days before taking any public action. This quiet delay gave him time to recover from the long journey, pray, and plan his next steps. Wise leaders know how to wait on God's timing instead of rushing ahead.

Nehemiah went out into the city under cover of night, taking only a few trusted men and a single animal to ride on. He had not yet told anyone what God had put in his heart to do for Jerusalem. By keeping quiet, he avoided tipping off enemies or causing panic before he had a clear plan.

He slipped out through the Valley Gate and traveled along the south side of the city toward the Serpent Well and the Dung Gate. Along the way, he carefully inspected the broken walls and the burned gates. He examined the ruins closely to understand the full size of the rebuilding task.

Nehemiah pressed forward toward the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool on the east side of the city. There the piles of stone and rubble were so deep and crowded that his mount could not pass through. The damage was far worse than what could be seen from afar.

Nehemiah continued on foot up the Kidron Valley in the darkness, continuing his survey of the damaged eastern wall. After completing his circuit around the city, he returned and reentered through the Valley Gate where he had started. He now had firsthand knowledge of all the work ahead.

The local rulers and Jewish leaders had no idea where Nehemiah had gone or what he was doing. He had kept his mission entirely quiet from the priests, nobles, and common workers. This careful secrecy prevented premature opposition while his preparations were still underway.

With his plans ready, Nehemiah called the people together and pointed out the desperate condition of the city. He identified himself with them, urging them to rebuild the burned walls so they would no longer live in shame and disgrace. Instead of blaming others, he invited everyone to share in the work.

Nehemiah encouraged the listeners by telling how God had graciously guided him and what the king had promised. Hearing this good news, the people responded eagerly, saying, 'Let us start rebuilding.' They encouraged one another and committed themselves to the good work.

Sanballat, Tobiah, and an Arab leader named Geshem heard that work was starting and openly mocked the Jews. They tried to scare the builders by accusing them of rebelling against the Persian king. Accusing God's people of treason was an old tactic used to halt the city's progress.

Nehemiah answered the mockers with quiet confidence, declaring that the God of heaven would give His servants success. He also told the enemies plainly that they had no historical, legal, or religious claim to Jerusalem. God's people were ready to move forward in faith, relying on the Lord rather than human approval.
